S1_incident_reporting.quote: Manufacturers shall report to the relevant regulator any thermal incident involving fire, injury, evacuation, emergency-service response, or material property damage within 24 hours of learning of it, and submit a complete incident report within 10 calendar days. Other overheating incidents requiring service or safety-related shutdown shall be reported within 30 days. Manufacturers shall notify affected customers within 48 hours of learning of an incident that presents a credible ongoing safety risk, and promptly provide any regulator-required safety instructions.

S2_thermal_testing.quote: Each model shall undergo a sustained-heat test at 55 °C using a regulator-approved sampling protocol. Manufacturers shall submit per-model results, including sample size and failure rate, to the relevant regulator. The manufacturer shall also provide those results to customers who buy that model, in a clear and accessible format. A result above 5% shall require a corrective-action plan and follow-up testing within a regulator-set period; it shall not by itself prohibit sale.

S3_remote_shutoff.quote: New home battery models shall include a remote emergency shut-off capability beginning 24 months after adoption of this standard. Existing installed units shall be upgraded where technically feasible within 72 months after adoption; manufacturers shall inform regulators of the number and share of units upgraded and any technical barriers.

S4_fire_suppression.quote: New home battery units shall include built-in fire suppression beginning 36 months after adoption of this standard. The requirement applies to units manufactured on or after that effective date; manufacturers shall provide regulators with documentation demonstrating compliance.

S5_customer_disclosure.quote: Model-specific 55 °C test results shall be provided directly to purchasers of that model in a clear, accessible format, but shall not be posted in a publicly accessible location; regulators may publish aggregate results. Manufacturers shall notify affected customers within 48 hours of learning of a credible ongoing safety risk, and promptly issue updated instructions or notices required by a regulator. A model-specific thermal incident rate exceeding 8 incidents per 100,000 installed units in any 12-month period, calculated from validated incident and exposure data, shall trigger prompt regulator review and a mandatory customer-facing recall or other regulator-approved safety remedy.

document.section_notes: The final rules require serious-incident reporting within 24 hours and other overheating within 30 days, but exclude minor incidents not requiring service. S2 sets a 55°C test and 5% threshold, yet exceeding it triggers only corrective action, not a sales ban; per-model results go to purchasers and regulators but not the public. S3 delays new-unit shut-off to 24 months and retrofit to 72 months with a feasibility escape; S4 requires built-in suppression at 36 months; S5 uses an 8/100k trigger with mandatory remedy but allows open-ended alternatives to recall.
